summary: Proposes an alternative to IPsec for securing signaling between a Mobile IPv6 mobile node and its home agent. It defines a mobility message authentication option that can be added to Binding Updates and Acknowledgements. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4285 describes shared-key options for authenticating Mobile IPv6 registration messages between a mobile device and its Home Agent or home AAA server. The IESG limits its recommended use to the networks described in the RFC's applicability statement.

questions: what is mobile ipv6 authentication option
alternative to ipsec for mobile ipv6
how does mobile ipv6 replay protection work
subtitle: A shared-key method for authenticating Mobile IPv6 registration messages in specific networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile IPv6 uses IPsec to protect registration between a Mobile Node and Home Agent, but some networks dynamically assign Home Agents and rely on a backend AAA security association.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines authentication options for Binding Updates and Acknowledgements using shared keys, with an optional timestamp option for replay protection.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and intended for the networks in its applicability statement. The IESG says the mechanism's security properties were not reviewed in the IETF and recommends against use outside those conditions.

today: RFC 4285 is an Informational RFC published in January 2006 and has not been obsoleted or updated according to the unit metadata. The IESG note recommends against using it outside the environments in its applicability statement.

sections.title: When the Alternative Applies
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 normally uses IPsec Security Associations between a Mobile Node (MN) and its Home Agent (HA) to protect Binding Update (BU) and Binding Acknowledgement (BA) messages. RFC 4285 describes another way to authenticate these messages without requiring the MN to establish an IPsec association with the HA.

The applicability statement describes networks where the HA and home address may be assigned dynamically, the long-term security association is with a backend AAA server, support for IKEv2 may be incomplete, or bandwidth constraints make fewer signaling messages desirable. CDMA networks are given as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: This method is for specific network settings where a mobile device may not have a long-term security association with its Home Agent. The RFC describes those settings in its applicability statement.

sections.title: Registration Message Exchange
sections.content:
The Mobile Node sends a Binding Update containing its identity option and the mobility message authentication option. It may also include the replay-protection option. The HA or home AAA server authenticates the Mobile Node and returns a Binding Acknowledgement with the applicable options.

The Mobile Node MUST identify itself using the MN-NAI form of the Mobile Node Identifier option. The RFC warns that this mechanism does not provide confidentiality for Return Routability messages or authentication and integrity protection for Mobile Prefix Discovery. Unless the network supplies those protections, it says Route Optimization and Mobile Prefix Discovery should not be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile device sends a signed registration request, and the Home Agent or AAA server checks it before replying. The RFC also identifies other Mobile IPv6 functions that this method does not protect.

sections.title: Mobility Message Authentication Option
sections.content:
The authentication option contains an option type, length, subtype, Mobility SPI, and authentication data. The RFC assigns option type 9. Subtype 1 authenticates between the Mobile Node and Home Agent; subtype 2 authenticates a Binding Update using a shared association with the home AAA server.

For the MN-HA subtype, the security association includes a 16-octet key and uses HMAC-SHA1. The authentication data uses the first 96 bits of the result. The MN-AAA subtype is used only in Binding Updates; the corresponding acknowledgement uses the MN-HA option.
sections.plainLanguage: The option carries a subtype that identifies which party shares the key. The sender and checker compute authentication data from the message and the shared key, then compare the result.

sections.title: Authentication Failure and Replay Protection
sections.content:
If authentication fails and a shared-key association exists, the Home Agent MUST send a Binding Acknowledgement with status MIPV6-AUTH-FAIL. After receiving this status, the Mobile Node SHOULD stop sending new Binding Updates.

The optional replay-protection option has type 10 and carries a 64-bit NTP-format timestamp. After authenticating a Binding Update, the Home Agent checks that the timestamp is close enough to its own clock and greater than timestamps it previously accepted for that node. A default comparison window of 7 seconds MAY be used. If the timestamp is invalid, the Home Agent sends MIPV6-ID-MISMATCH and does not create a binding entry.
sections.plainLanguage: A failed authentication produces an error response. An optional timestamp helps the Home Agent reject an old request that someone tries to replay.

sections.title: Security Review and IESG Warning
sections.content:
The RFC describes the new options as an alternative to IPsec for authenticating Binding Updates and Acknowledgements. Replay protection is optional and can use the timestamp option.

The IESG note says this RFC is not a candidate for an Internet Standard and that the mechanism's security properties were not reviewed in the IETF. It recommends against use outside environments meeting the applicability statement and advises a sufficient security review before deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG warns that this mechanism was not reviewed for Internet Standard use. The RFC recommends limiting it to the stated environments and reviewing its security for each deployment.
